clue.text: Ulysses remake represented modern-day exiles

indicators.note: to represent is to present again, so the letters of the two words are presented anew in a different order

explanation.surface: A new version of Joyce's Ulysses portrayed today's displaced people.
explanation.walkthrough: 'remake' looks like the anagram signal for Ulysses, but it is fodder too: the thirteen letters of ULYSSES and REMAKE together are rearranged, with 'represented' as the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: People fleeing their homelands and requesting refuge abroad are the exiles of the present day.

clue.text: Pretend group performed in theatre?

definitions.meaning: a fictional heavy metal band from a 1984 mockumentary film
a lumbar puncture, a medical procedure carried out in an operating theatre

explanation.walkthrough: 'theatre' suggests the stage, where a pretend group would play, but here it is the hospital operating theatre.
explanation.definitionFit: The name belongs both to a spoof rock band in a mock documentary and to a lumbar puncture procedure.

clue.text: Without these I'm it

parts.note: take away the first and last letters, the boundaries, of the word wanted and what remains reads as the phrase I'm it

explanation.walkthrough: Strip the outer letters (the boundaries) of the answer and IMIT is left, read as "I'm it".
explanation.definitionFit: Limits are boundaries or extremes, and here they are the outermost letters of the word itself.

clue.text: Bloke has to leave vegetables

parts.note: a bloke is an informal word for a man
to get out is to leave

explanation.surface: A man is told he must go, perhaps from the vegetable patch.
explanation.definitionFit: Mangetout are flat edible pea pods eaten whole, a kind of vegetable; the word serves as its own plural.

clue.text: Dames popular with sailors?

definitions.meaning: the Norfolk waterways, lakes and rivers in eastern England much used for sailing holidays

explanation.walkthrough: The Norfolk Broads are a network of rivers and lakes in eastern England popular for boating.
explanation.definitionFit: Broads is US slang for women, like dames, and also names the Norfolk lakes where people sail.

clue.text: Count brass (mine regularly goes missing)

indicators.note: every other letter of the words brass and mine drops out, leaving the alternate ones

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's mine produces brass only some of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Count' looks like a verb or a nobleman, but it is the title of the jazz bandleader.
explanation.definitionFit: Count Basie was the celebrated American jazz bandleader, so Count calls up his surname.

clue.text: Obsessive finds love on the web a source of pain

parts.note: love is nil in tennis scoring, which looks like the letter O
the web is the internet, the net
the rack is a torture device, a source of pain

explanation.surface: Someone fixated on internet romance finds it torturous.
explanation.definitionFit: A one-track mind thinks of only one thing, the hallmark of being obsessive.

clue.text: Eejit in America taken in by weel-faur'd wee bletherskate

indicators.note: the run of letters sits inside the words that follow, taken into them

explanation.surface: A Scots-flavoured insult: a fool held captive by a good-looking little chatterbox.
explanation.walkthrough: The Scots words mean well-favoured (good-looking) and a babbling fool; eejit is Irish and Scots for idiot.
explanation.definitionFit: Dweeb is American slang for a boring, socially inept person, the US counterpart of an eejit.

clue.text: One is getting skinny without essential nutrient

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so skinny goes round the other piece

parts.note: skinny means thin
the speaker saying one is becomes I am

explanation.surface: A person grows thin through lacking a vital nutrient.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' reads as lacking, but here it means outside: I AM goes inside THIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Thiamin is vitamin B1, a nutrient the body cannot make and needs from food.

clue.text: English actress's assets for part of the political system

parts.note: Thora Hird, an English actress, written with her initial as T Hird
a person's estate is all their assets

explanation.surface: The property of a British actress appears as a piece of constitutional machinery.
explanation.walkthrough: Thora Hird was a much-loved English comic actress; her initial and surname make T HIRD.
explanation.definitionFit: The Third Estate was the commons, one of the three estates of the realm alongside clergy and nobility.

clue.text: See 1
Management employing waitress with PhD

indicators.note: to employ letters is to put them to use in a new arrangement, so the waitress and PhD letters are reordered

explanation.surface: A restaurant manager hires a waitress who holds a doctorate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'employing' seems to mean hiring the waitress, but it signals that her letters, with PHD, are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Stewardship is the careful running or supervision of something, that is, its management.

clue.text: I have ruled as tsar, haven't I?

parts.note: a muddled, terrible version of the first part of the answer gives these words, so the answer itself is wordplay producing them

explanation.surface: A Russian ruler boasts of his reign.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse anagram: the first seven letters of the answer, given an anagram signal ('terrible', the last word of the answer), produce the clue's "haven't I".
explanation.definitionFit: The sixteenth-century Russian Ivan IV was the first ruler crowned tsar, speaking here in the first person.

clue.text: Does once make orthographical mistake

definitions.meaning: an archaic form of the verb does, as in old poetry
to put a dot over the letter H, where only i should be dotted, is a spelling slip

explanation.walkthrough: Split the answer as DOT H: dotting an H instead of an i is the orthographical mistake.
explanation.definitionFit: Doth is the old third-person form of do, and read as two words it describes dotting the wrong letter.

clue.text: Sadly concur more than half of drugs can be found in abundance

indicators.note: sadly here means in a sorry, messed-up state, so the letters of concur are rearranged
only four of the seven letters are kept, more than half, dropping the end

parts.note: opiates are drugs derived from opium

explanation.surface: Someone reluctantly agrees that most drugs are plentiful.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sadly' turns CONCUR into CORNUC; 'more than half of' keeps OPIA from OPIATES, cutting TES.
explanation.definitionFit: A cornucopia is the horn of plenty, an emblem of abundance, and so a plentiful supply.

clue.text: Doctor only ignoring adult's rather trapped wind

indicators.note: one piece is shut inside the other, as if caught in a trap
to doctor is to tamper with, so the letters of only are altered
ignoring means leaving out, so a letter is dropped from rather

parts.note: A is the film-classification abbreviation for adult

explanation.surface: A medic deals only with an adult's embarrassing flatulence.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a medical consultation about flatulence; 'wind' is really a noun for a breeze from the north, and 'adult' is the film-certificate letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A northerly is a wind blowing from the north, so the word works as a noun for wind.

clue.text: Constant review of university in recent study

indicators.note: to review is to view again, here backwards, so the whole run of pieces is read from the end
university goes inside the recent piece

parts.note: recent means late, as in the late news
prep is British school slang for homework or private study

explanation.surface: A steady appraisal of a university appears in a new piece of research.
explanation.walkthrough: 'review of' turns the whole run LAUTEPREP backwards; PREP is homework time at a British boarding school.
explanation.definitionFit: Perpetual means unceasing or never-ending, which is constant in its sense of continual.

clue.text: Moved like the wind around end of haunted outhouse

indicators.note: the moving piece goes around the single letter, enclosing it

parts.note: to woosh, or whoosh, is to rush past with a rushing sound, like the wind

indicators.note: the last letter of haunted is taken

explanation.surface: A gust swept round the end of a spooky garden shed.
explanation.walkthrough: Cold Comfort Farm's 'something nasty in the woodshed' gives the haunted feel; D goes inside WOOSHED.
explanation.definitionFit: A woodshed is a small outbuilding for storing firewood, a kind of outhouse.

clue.text: They love football team's jockstraps?

definitions.meaning: athletic garments that hold things up

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second sense: a jockstrap literally supports.
explanation.definitionFit: Fans who back a club are its supporters, and athletic jockstraps are supporters in the sense of garments that hold up.

clue.text: It's nasty, brutish, short

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, losing its final letter

parts.note: brutish means crude, coarse and uncivilised

explanation.surface: An echo of Hobbes's line that life is nasty, brutish and short.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' clips the last letter E from CRUDE. Thomas Hobbes described life in the state of nature as nasty, brutish and short.
explanation.definitionFit: Crud is slang for dirt or filth, any unpleasant and nasty substance.

clue.text: Amateur race which is dangerous, being over the limit in Escort

indicators.note: in a down answer one piece stands above the next, so this is placed over the final piece

parts.note: the TT is the Isle of Man Tourist Trophy motorcycle race, notoriously dangerous
the end is the limit or furthest point

explanation.surface: A dangerous amateur race after drinking over the limit, in a Ford Escort car.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital in 'Escort' points at the Ford car, a red herring; 'being over' puts A and TT above END in the down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: To attend someone is to accompany them, as an escort does.

clue.text: Extremely dangerous and revolting, the trematode devours other's innards

indicators.note: the anagrammed letters swallow the inner piece, taking it inside
revolting means rising up in revolt, so the letters overturn into a new order
the inner letters, dropping the first and last

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: A disgusting parasitic flatworm eats the guts of another.
explanation.walkthrough: A trematode is a parasitic fluke. 'innards' takes THE from the middle of OTHER; 'revolting' mixes THE TREMATODE, which 'devours' THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone armed to the teeth carries many weapons and so is extremely dangerous.

clue.text: Diminutive, fat and married to Homer

definitions.meaning: a short form of margarine, a spread
the wife of Homer Simpson in the cartoon The Simpsons

explanation.walkthrough: Homer is the cartoon father in The Simpsons, not the Greek poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Marge is short for margarine, a cooking fat, and the name of Homer Simpson's wife.

clue.text: In the manner of 1, 9 — perhaps in a strange way

definitions.meaning: one and nine are examples of odd numbers, so in their manner

explanation.walkthrough: '1, 9' looks like a cross-reference to the linked across answer, but it is just the numbers one and nine, which are odd.
explanation.definitionFit: Oddly means strangely, and odd numbers such as one and nine behave in an odd manner.

clue.text: After essentially easeful death, poor beggar's finally buried and returned to the ground

indicators.note: the rest follows the middle letter, coming after it
the essence or heart of the word, its middle letter
one letter is buried inside the rearranged letters
poor means in bad shape, so the letters of death are rearranged
the last letter of beggar's is taken

explanation.surface: A poor man, after a peaceful death, is finally laid in his grave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essentially' takes E from the middle of EASEFUL; 'poor' turns DEATH into ATHED, and R ('finally' from beggar's) is 'buried' in it.
explanation.definitionFit: An electrical device that is earthed has been connected back to the ground.

clue.text: Devotee starts to find Lady Gaga unbearably boring

parts.note: the opening letters of devotee, its starts, used as a plural noun

indicators.note: gaga means crazy or senile, so the letters of lady go haywire

explanation.surface: A fan begins to find a pop star tiresome.
explanation.walkthrough: Arachne confirmed 'starts' is a plural noun, the starting letters DE of Devotee; 'Gaga' scrambles LADY into ADLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Deadly is colloquial for extremely dull, as in a deadly boring evening.

clue.text: Country bumpkins died for the king, making horrible noises

indicators.note: for means in place of, so one letter replaces another

parts.note: yokels are unsophisticated country people
K is the chess abbreviation for king
D is the abbreviation for died, as in genealogies

explanation.surface: Rustics gave their lives for the monarch, wailing as they went.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for' puts D (died) in place of K (king) in YOKELS.
explanation.definitionFit: Yodels are warbling Alpine calls that swing between registers, which some hear as horrible noises.
